entries.title: 2016 Cubs roundtable: World Series stars take fresh look back at just how good team really was
entries.summary: <p>Dexter Fowler can’t believe how long it has been since the “Welcome to the team!” texts poured in before the 2016 season.</p><p>They came from Manny Machado, Adam Jones, Ubaldo Jimenez and others — all members of the Orioles — after some erroneous reporting in the media. A couple of days later, the free-agent outfielder re-signed with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and then hid in a car for 15 minutes at the team’s spring training complex before strolling onto the field and surprising his stunned pals.</p><p>“One of the happiest moments of my life, the love I felt,” the former leadoff hitter says now.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >curse-busting World Series championship awaited all of them</a>, the memories made along the way of the sort that last forever.</p><p>Game 7 starter Kyle Hendricks still laughs at himself for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/04/12/kyle-kendricks-cubs-angels-2016-world-series-cleveland-nlcs-dodgers-joe-maddon" target="_blank" >following Jon Lester and John Lackey around like a lost puppy</a> and treasures the way Jake Arrieta looked out for him. Game 6 winner Arrieta still misses dinners on the road that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/22/2016-cubs-great-jake-arrieta-reflects-on-unforgettable-run-on-top-of-the-pitching-world" target="_blank" >never felt quite the same on any other team</a>. Series MVP Ben Zobrist still can’t forget — or stop howling about — the sight of first baseman Anthony Rizzo’s bare behind as he stood with his arms in the air like Rocky Balboa and fired up the clubhouse before Games 5, 6 and 7 against the Guardians.</p><p>Nothing beats those old stories, if — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >almost exactly 10 years since the Cubs stormed the mound in Cleveland</a> — we can call them “old.”</p><p>But how do the Cubs reflect on what happened on the field? We discussed that with Arrieta, Fowler, Hendricks, Zobrist, staff ace Lester and the reliever who got the last out in Game 7, Mike Montgomery. Here’s some of what they said, lightly edited for clarity:</p><h3><b>Were the 2016 Cubs the best team you ever played for?</b></h3><p><b>Fowler: </b>“Yes, 100%. Just on paper, really, really good. Also in the locker room, everybody was always together. Those are brothers and always will be brothers for life.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“It’s hard to say the best; it depends who the opposition is. If we were facing a real power pitching team, I think the 2015 Royals would’ve been the best; we were tough to strike out. But if you put that Cubs offense against the Royals, it’s going to be a fight because the Cubs hit some bombs. Neck and neck, just different in regard to how we won games.”</p><p><b>Lester: </b>“I think talent-wise, the 2007 Red Sox were probably the best team I’ve ever seen on the field. Depth in the lineup, in the rotation, in the bullpen, a lockdown closer; it was pretty impressive. And then I would probably put the 2013 Red Sox and the 2016 Cubs as a little bit of a tie. I think ’16 had more talent than ’13, but as far as just fun and the best groups I’ve been around, I would put them as a tie. In ’13 we had a bunch of rejects on one-year deals, end of careers, supposedly in a rebuild, but got a bunch of lunatics together and said, ‘Hey, that sounds good’ and then went and won.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“Yes, for sure — in so many different ways. Best team I’ve ever played for, best guys I’ve ever played with, best coaching, best players, best everything.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/chicago-cubs-world-series-2016-team-story-10-years-later" target="_blank" >10 years after: How Cubs went from lovable losers to 2016 World Series champions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3><b>Where do those Cubs belong in the pecking order of World Series champions?</b></h3><p><b>Arrieta: </b>“In terms of where we stack up talent-wise, probably not at the top, but it’s not always about that. It’s about coming through in the most pivotal of moments. Also, I think what made us so good was the personalities and the character behind that team. Relationships and lifelong friendships are what made us so special. If we don’t have those bonds, we don’t perform the same way on the field, I guarantee that.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“In a single-season setting, we were a great team. It’s hard to put that in the scope of baseball, though. Our focus was so solely around the city of Chicago, the 108 years. We wanted to be the greatest team for Chicago in the context of history.”</p><p><b>Lester: </b>“This is a very politically correct answer, but I feel like anybody who ever won a championship ought to be tied for first. The way we figured out how to pull the rope at the same time, that was rare.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“I would put that team up against any team in history as far as the clutch ability to come back from the brink in the midst of the most pressure any team has faced.”</p><p><b>Fowler: </b>“We were stacked — no holes. Our pitching staff, our lineup, Cy Youngs and All-Stars up and down, it was crazy. We had seven All-Stars that year, and five of us were starters. You play us seven games against any of these Dodgers teams, we’re winning at least four of those.”</p><p><b>Montgomery: </b>“I would say it was one of the top three to five championship runs by a team in baseball ever solely due to the ‘curse.’ But also there were all the personalities. Someone like me as an unsung hero? The David Ross situation in Game 7? I don’t think it’s about who was better, though. You’ll never know, and it’s a dead-end argument.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Xl3iZpcAb2g?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago Cubs World Series Highlights 2016!"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Who was the best — or most important — player on that Cubs team?</b></h3><p><b>Fowler: </b>“Most important and best is totally different to me. On paper, Kris Bryant was the best player. But most important? It’s a toss-up. We had some pitchers, man.”</p><p><b>Arrieta: </b>“That’s very hard to answer. Jason Heyward’s leadership and selflessness, there’s an MVP in that. Anthony Rizzo’s and David Ross’ vocal leadership were priceless. The way Jon Lester led by example was, too. Same with Dexter with his smile and charisma and energy. I can’t pick one.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“Rizzo and Bryant, from a position-player standpoint, were irreplaceable. KB was the MVP of the league; how he played defense and ran the bases gave the other team so much to think about. Together, that tandem, they made pitchers have to work so hard that by the time they got to me, if I was batting cleanup, they were too tired to focus on me. We needed those two to come through, and they did. Those two were the backbone of our lineup.”</p><h3><b>Are you surprised those Cubs never made it back to a World Series?</b></h3><p><b>Lester: </b>“It’s a little surprising, but baseball’s hard. In 2017, we still had a great team and we competed, but we may have run out of some steam. I think the guys that were in it understand how hard it is to do it again. Look at the teams spending more money than everybody else. You have to go out and spend that kind of money year in and year out to get the pieces you need. But I am surprised we didn’t at least get back into another one.”</p><p><b>Hendricks: </b>“I think the expectation was you get there and go back to the playoffs and ‘This is how it happens.’ You don’t realize how hard it is at the time. It always leaves you wanting more, wanting that feeling again. Our group remained so special, but, yeah, it was disappointing.”</p><p><b>Montgomery: </b>“Deep down, I thought we had the team for three to five years where we should’ve won multiple World Series. There was always a feeling of, ‘What if?’ It just makes me appreciate that ’16 team even more.”</p><p><b>Fowler: </b>“I think if we all stayed together — all of us — we would’ve won multiple.”</p><p><b>Zobrist: </b>“I knew 2017 was going to be an uphill climb; everybody was exhausted at the beginning. I was more disappointed in 2018 and 2019. I really thought we had a chance both years. I was surprised we didn’t get there. entries.title: Boo, who? College football's Halloween Saturday promises more October spookiness
entries.summary: <p>A Week 9 Halloween Saturday in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >college football</a>?</p><p>It’s rather anticlimactic, at least in terms of boos and frights.</p><p>That’s because the top teams in the country already spent much of October holding on to the walls in a desperate attempt — failing, in many cases — to make it through a haunted house of a month without soiling themselves.</p><p>In Week 6, No. 1 Texas lost to unranked Oklahoma, LSU lost to unranked Kentucky and popular national championship pick Oregon lost at home to unranked UCLA.</p><p>In Week 7, No. 1 Georgia lost at home to unranked Auburn, Texas lost at home to unranked Florida and three other presumed title contenders — Notre Dame, Indiana and Alabama — went down.</p><p>And in Week 8, No. 2 BYU fell at unranked UCF while Texas Tech, Tennessee, Iowa and USC all took it on the chin from unranked foes.</p><p>The “unranked” thing has become one of the dominant themes of a season in which upsets — otherwise known as bad losses — have been the norm and only three unbeaten teams remain, well below what’s usually the case as November nears. Does anybody out there really think No. 1 Miami, No. 9 UCLA and No. 10 Utah will avoid getting dinged eventually? Put me down for a “no” on all three.</p><p>It boggles the mind to think about the College Football Playoff committee eventually managing to seed the 12-team tournament to anyone’s satisfaction. The disagreement — speaking of boos — might be louder and lustier than ever.</p><p>Meanwhile, the “unranked” thing has seeped all the way into my addled brain as I consider my predictions for this weekend’s games. A trick or a treat? Heck, I don’t know. Just take the Milk Duds and get off my stoop.</p><h3><b>Week 9 picks</b></h3><p><i>All games Saturday; my picks to cover listed first.</i></p><p><b>Illinois (-2½) at Maryland </b>(11 a.m., FS1, 890-AM): Playing in place of injured quarterback Katin Houser, Michael Clayton last week became only the third Illini true freshman ever to win a start, a 21-10 upset of Oregon. Clayton threw for only 84 yards in that game, though, which won’t cut it on the road — not even against the dysfunctional Terrapins, who are down a head coach after Mike Locksley was fired. Middies get smacked around but cover in Foxborough, Mass.</p><p><b>No. 22 Arizona (+3½) at No. 13 Texas Tech </b>(11 a.m., ESPN): Everybody is talking about Texas Tech billionaire booster Cody Campbell, who is putting the pressure on the one-loss Red Raiders, but the quiet truth is their one-loss visitors have the better season résumé and more mojo coming in. Give me the Wildcats in overtime.</p><p><b>Iowa (-3½) vs. No. 25 Wisconsin </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): The Badgers come in hot — their defense is playing lights-out — but it’s the Hawkeyes who have owned the Heartland Trophy series of late and have won the last three matchups in Iowa City by an average of over 22 points. Hawkeyes in a classic knuckle-dragger, 20-13.</p><p><b>No. 17 Florida (+12½) vs. No. 3 Georgia </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): The neutral-site game, forever and a day held in Jacksonville, Fla., has moved to Atlanta for the first time, which doesn’t seem all that neutral. Both teams had an extra week to prepare for the Cocktail Party. Bulldogs, 31-21.</p><p><b>USC (+6½) vs. No. 2 Ohio State </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5): Put the Buckeyes on upset alert because they’re starting a freshman QB, Luke Fahey, who has neither been there nor done that and now, with star Julian Sayin out, gets the nod for the first time. It’s not like the Buckeyes can just lean into their rushing attack, which has been so-so. The Trojans have a shot, but I’ll take the visitors by less than the spread.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>Oregon (-3) vs. No. 20 Northwestern </b>(2:30 p.m., Peacock, 720-AM): The Ducks are a bit of a mess, but the indignity of that — along with their speed and home turf — should propel them against an opponent that has traveled a mighty long way to get there. Ducks by double digits.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>North Carolina (+14½) vs. No. 1 Miami </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): The whole season has been weird. Bill Belichick coaching college ball will never not be weird. Give me more weird. Tar Heels in an upset that makes utterly no sense at all.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>4-1 straight-up, 3-2 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>41-15 straight-up, 31-25 against the spread.</p>

Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddyoil-l-d/" target="_blank" >Billions of gallons of raw sewage are pouring into the Chicago River after storms </a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddyoil-l-h/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a></h5><p><b>Smell test</b>: After heavy rain, Chicagoans near Bubbly Creek have come to expect putrid smells from the small body of water that marks the South Fork of the Chicago River and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park. The odor is from raw sewage in the creek. Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline.</p><p><b>Why is this happening?</b>: In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer. That water should run through a sewage pumping station and be moved to a treatment facility. But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago dumps untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.</p><p><b>The scale</b>: This year, the sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue near Bridgeport has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. The North Branch pumping station, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square, has spewed nearly two billion gallons of untreated sewage into the North Branch of the Chicago River this year.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Climate change is contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. The intense rain overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes. Chicago's sewer system can handle just two inches of rain before flooding is likely. All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the North Branch of the river threatens wildlife and poses health risks for people with weak immune systems.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddyoil-l-k/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>LET’S DISCUSS 🌧️</h4><p>We're hosting a community dinner and discussion about why flooding is getting worse in Chicago on Thursday, Nov. 12 at the Garfield Park Field House.</p><p>Have you experienced flooding? Do you have questions about how the city is addressing this issue — and how to protect your health and home? We'll have experts discuss on a panel moderated by Sun-Times reporter Brett Chase.</p><p>Learn more and reserve a spot for this free event <a class="Link" entries.title: What to know about voting by mail in Illinois like Pope Leo did. Is it legal and how do you do it?
entries.summary: <p>Chicago-born <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv" ><u>Pope Leo XIV</u></a>, a registered voter in Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/10/29/pope-leo-xiv-mail-ballot-illinois-midterm-election" >has voted by mail ahead of midterm elections</a> on Nov. 3, the Sun-Times reported. The Vatican on Friday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/10/30/vatican-pope-leo-voted-midterm-elections-mail-ballot-chicago" >confirmed he has submitted his mail ballot in Illinois</a>. The Vatican also confirmed that the pope “exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so,” including when he lived in Peru.</p><h3>Is voting by mail legal? How does it work?</h3><p>Yes, it’s legal.</p><p>Any Illinois registered voter can vote by mail, said the Illinois State Board of Elections. And U.S. citizens who are overseas have the right to vote by mail with a law called UOCAVA, The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act. The law is mostly for the military, but it’s also for U.S. citizens who are overseas.</p><p>Until 2010, Illinois voters had to have an excuse to get what was then called an “absentee ballot.”</p><p>Now, “any Illinois registered voter can vote by mail,” said Matt Dietrich, spokesman for the Illinois State Board of Elections.</p><h3><b>Is it too late to vote by mail in Illinois’ midterm election?</b></h3><p>Not if you applied by Oct. 29 to do so. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day will be counted by Illinois election authorities as long as they're received within two weeks (by Nov. 17). But the deadline to apply for a mail ballot has passed; that window was open from Aug. 5 until Oct. 29. Otherwise you'll either have to head an early voting site or to your local precinct on Nov. 3.</p><p>Pope Leo, registered as Robert Francis Prevost in New Lenox, made his request on Oct. 3, the Will County clerk’s office said.</p><h3><b>Has President Donald Trump tried to restrict voting by mail?</b></h3><p>Yes. But in Illinois, it’s “business as usual,” for voting by mail, Cook County Clerk Monica Gordon said in August.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/20/mail-voting-illinois-explainer-trump" ><u>Nothing has changed with the state’s mail ballot plan</u></a>, even though legal challenges abound, the Illinois State Board of Elections said in August.</p><p>Through an executive order, legal challenges and efforts in Congress, Trump has tried to cast doubt and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/26/illinois-ag-kwame-raoul-lawsuit-postal-service-mail-ballot-rule-midterm-elections" ><u>restrict mail ballots</u></a>, which he has falsely blamed for his 2020 loss.</p><p>Despite his fight against mail-in voting Trump voted by mail again in Florida’s Republican primary. He also voted by mail in a special election in Palm Beach County earlier this year.</p><p>In September, the U.S. Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail voting, said the <a class="Link" href="https://votingrightslab.org/2026/09/17/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-proposed-usps-mail-ballot-rule/" target="_blank" ><u>Voting Rights Lab</u></a>.</p><p>The decision means that all 50 states can continue to use their existing processes for mail voting, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/u-s-supreme-court-blocks-postal-service-from-restricting-mail-ballots" target="_blank" ><u>ACLU</u></a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/how-to-vote-illinois-general" >How to vote in the November 2026 Illinois general election</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Northwestern physicists trapped an antimatter particle in a lab for months. Here's why it matters
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern physicists have figured out how to trap a fast-moving, fickle particle that is notoriously difficult to study. </p><p>The scientists used electric and magnetic fields to capture, freeze and store a single positron — the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Their experiment, published early this month in the journal <a class="Link" href="https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/gbkc-6nlj" target="_blank" >Physical Review Letters</a>, allowed them to study antimatter in a controlled quantum state for months at a time. </p><p>Their discovery could make or break a longstanding theory in physics about how our universe was formed, Gerald Gabrielse the study's lead author and the director of Northwestern's Center for Fundamental Physics said. </p><p>"[Our work] has really captured a tremendous amount of scientific and public attention," Gabrielse said.</p><p>Matter — the stuff we're all made out of — contains three particles: electrons, protons and neutrons. Each of those particles also has a twin antimatter particle with the opposite electrical charge. A positron has a positive charge, while an electron has a negative charge. Whenever matter and antimatter touch, they "annihilate" each other, disappearing and turning into energy. </p><p>That's why it's so hard to capture antimatter, Gabrielse said. To capture it, he explained, you need a container without walls. </p><p>Gabrielse and his team created such a container with batteries and magnets to hold and freeze the positron in a resting state so that it couldn't touch anything. They call it a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." </p><p>"This allowed us to observe the positron, its energy levels and take really precise measurements," Gabrielse said. </p><p>Now that Gabrielse and his team are able to observe and control a positron, they can take those measurements of its magnetic properties and compare them to a normal electron. </p><p>According to the Standard Model of particle physics, positrons should be perfect mirror images of electrons. If the positron's measurements don't match an electron's, it could poke a hole in the Standard Model, which explains why our universe looks the way it does.</p><p>"The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter," Gabrielse said. "But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we’d be left with nothing. There’s clearly something wrong with that theory, and that’s what we’re trying to figure out."</p><p>And this new research could go beyond basic science.</p><p>"It would also help explain the universe and invent new technologies," Gabrielse said. "Experiments like this are motivation to try to get a better way to describe our universe."</p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, robbed 8 people at gunpoint in under 2 hours over summer, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy is accused of robbing eight people at gunpoint in under two hours last summer in neighborhoods across the city, Chicago police said. </p><p>The teen was arrested Thursday and cited in a juvenile petition with eight felony counts of armed robbery and one count of possessing a stolen vehicle, Chicago police said. </p><p>Between 5:30 a.m. and 7:15 a.m. Aug. 9, the teen allegedly robbed eight people at gunpoint in the Loop, Brighton Park, Back of the Yards and West Pullman, officials said. The individuals ranged in age from 21 to 62. </p><p>The boy was was expected to appear in court Friday. </p>

entries.title: New Bears DT Jeffery Simmons will wear No. 99, expected to play Monday vs. Seahawks
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> got new defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in Halas Hall on Thursday and expect to have him on the field when they visit the Seahawks on Monday.</p><p>General manager Ryan Poles said he would leave that decision to coach Ben Johnson, but "would assume" Simmons will make his Bears debut Monday.</p><p>The team announced he will wear No. 99, the same as Hall of Fame defensive lineman Dan Hampton.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/29/more-than-anything-else-bears-trade-for-dt-jeffery-simmons-says-they-think-qb-caleb-williams-has-arrived" >The Bears traded two first-round picks to the Titans for Simmons</a> hoping he'd further propel what they anticipate to be a Super Bowl run.</p><p>Simmons, 29, has made four Pro Bowls and was an All-Pro last season. In eight seasons with the Titans, he has 46 1/2 sacks, nine forced fumbles and 414 total tackles. He had four sacks in seven games for them this season.</p><p>This was the third major trade-deadline acquisition for Poles, who dealt a second-round pick for Steelers wide receiver Chase Claypool in 2022 and a second-rounder to the Commanders for defensive end Montez Sweat the next year. He also traded linebacker Roquan Smith to the Ravens for a second-round pick in 2022.</p>

entries.title: Sam Chatman, DJ known as the Godfather of Steppin', dies at 85
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Popular disc jockey Sam Chatman was known as the Godfather of Steppin' because he coined the term that summed up the popular dance genre that was born in Chicago.</p><p>Its distinctive flow involves dance partners separating and then smoothly walking or spinning back to each other.</p><p>The dance evolved from Bopping, and Mr. Chatman, after seeing his friend add the smooth boomerang element at a West Side club one night in the '70s, exclaimed his approval by stating "Step on!"</p><p>Steppin' became a style of its own and grew a wide fan base around Chicago and the country. It experienced a rebirth in the early 2000s with popular music pointing back to the classic style.</p><p>"It's sort of a ballroom type dance with a twist to it," said Mr. Chatman's son Marlon Chatman.</p><p>Mr. Chatman began spinning at parties as an underclassman at Crane High School and continued after he graduated and began working for the CTA as a bus driver.</p><p>He promoted his DJ sets by leaving flyers on the seats of the bus he drove.</p><p>"One day his supervisor told him 'I heard what you're doing, and you need to stop or you're going to get fired,'" recalled Mr. Chatman's daughter Samantha Chatman, a news anchor and investigative reporter with ABC 7 Chicago.</p><p>"He told her 'I'll make you a deal, I'll give you VIP to all my parties if you let this slide.' And she agreed," Mr. Chatman's daughter said.</p><p>Mr. Chatman continued to DJ after retiring from the CTA and even live streamed sets during the pandemic.</p><p>"I wanted him to slow down a bit as he got older, but he was like 'Why would I stop doing what I love?' And how can you argue with that?" his daughter said.</p><p>Mr. Chatman died Oct. 22 from natural causes. He was 85.</p><p>He performed a DJ set the week before he passed away.</p><p>"He was a very gentle and kind spirit," his daughter said. </p><p>Steppin' music ranges from The Temptations to Luther Vandross and Michael Jackson and hip-hop.</p><p>Mr. Chatman's encouraging tagline to his audience was always "Let's go to work."</p><p>He believed in being "steppers sharp" with natty suits and spit shine shoes.</p><p>Samantha Chatman recalled participating in a fraternity pageant while attending the University of Illinois and inviting her father to come.</p><p>"I said 'Dad, maybe wear an orange tie' because it's the school color. He wore an orange suit instead. And I look out in the audience, and my eyes just go wide, and and then I look at my mom and I'm like 'How could you let him? You've got to be kidding me.' But I should have known," she recalled with a laugh.</p><p>She planned to attend the Soul Train Music Awards in Chicago on Nov. 27 with her dad as her date.</p><p>"I don't know if I can bear to go," she said. "I am very crushed. This is the worst heartache I've ever felt. He was so excited to go."</p><p>Mr. Chatman put a microphone in his daughter's hand at a young age. He encouraged her to take on emcee duties at free Halloween parties he hosted at a South Side venue for kids to have a safe place to eat, munch candy and dance.</p><p>"He'd tell me things like 'Look at the audience, hold the microphone like this, don't bite your tongue,'" she said.</p><p>Mr. Chatman, who lived in the South Suburbs in recent years, was also a monster Bears fan.</p><p>"He did not play when it came to the Bears, and like many, they dictated his mood for the day," she said.</p><p>"He was such a nice man. That's the biggest thing I can say about him. He wanted others to feel special and connected," she said.</p><p>In addition to his son and daughter, Mr. Chatman is survived by his wife, Eva Chatman; his daughters Cynthia Stewart, Rita Chatman, Donna Fuller and Kyra Chatman; his son Kevin Gore; and multiple grandchildren and great grandchildren. He was preceded in death by his son Keith Gore.</p><p>A visitation will take place from 5 to 8 p.m. Friday at Leak and Sons Funeral Home at 18400 S. Pulaski Road, Country Club Hills. A wake will take place at 10 a.m. on Saturday at House of Hope, 752 E. 114th St., Chicago, with a celebration of life to follow at 11 a.m.</p>

entries.title: What to know about the 2026 Illinois State Report Card and how schools in Chicago fared on key metrics
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/30/2026-illinois-state-report-card-released-by-isbe-with-data-on-cps-schools/" target="_blank" ><i>originally published</i></a><i> by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at </i><a class="Link" href="https://ckbe.at/newsletters" target="_blank" ><i><u>ckbe.at/newsletters</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><p>After the Illinois State Board of Education changed the parameters for how it measures school-level performance earlier this year, the number of public schools in the state that are considered Exemplary — the state’s highest of five ratings — rose 17%</p><p>States are required by federal law to have an accountability system monitoring how schools perform on certain metrics. Under the previous system, only the top 10% of public schools in the state could achieve Exemplary status. Officials said that led to <a class="Link" href="http://google.com/url?q=https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/12/03/illinois-state-board-pushes-back-deadline-school-accountability/&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1793251694327413&usg=AOvVaw2WNZRMnExJqcI05K4JCfU9" target="_blank" ><u>a lopsided distribution of schools</u></a> stuck in the Commendable category — formerly the second-highest category. Now, 27% are considered Exemplary.</p><p>A new trove of data annually released as the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisreportcard.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Report Card</u></a> also shows an uptick in the percentage of students considered proficient in reading and math. Roughly 56% of students are considered proficient in English language arts, while almost 40% are in math. That’s up from 53% and 38.5%, respectively.</p><p>Years prior to 2025 cannot be compared because last year, the state <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/08/13/illinois-approves-lower-cut-scores-on-state-exams/" target="_blank" ><u>lowered the scores</u></a> needed to be deemed proficient in English language arts and math.</p><p>Illinois school leaders and Chicago are touting record-high graduation rates. The state recorded a four-year graduation rate of nearly 89%, a little less than a one percentage point increase from last year. In CPS, graduation rates also saw positive movement after <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/21/cps-2026-graduation-rate-increases-to-83-percent/" target="_blank" ><u>increasing for the second consecutive year from 82.5% in 2025 to more than 83%</u></a> in 2026.</p><p>“The fact that we're seeing the progress we are on a number of fronts is good news,” said Robin Steans, president of education advocacy group Advance Illinois.</p><p>The number of teachers in Illinois also continues to expand, now at nearly 144,000. Class sizes are generally trending downward, and the teacher retention rate is over 90% for the first time in over a decade. But teacher attendance rates are a cause for concern after they took a hit from the pandemic. In 2019, most Illinois teachers had high attendance — with 73% missing fewer than 10 days of school. Now, about 65% of teachers are in that category.</p><p>Here are three trends worth diving into from this year’s latest state report card data.</p><h3><b>New state rating system opens door to exemplary status</b></h3><p>One of the biggest differences families may notice about this year’s data is the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/04/15/illinois-approves-new-school-accountability-system/" target="_blank" ><u>new way Illinois categorizes public schools’ performance</u></a>.</p><p>Instead of weighing schools against each other, schools are placed in one of five groups — Exemplary, Approaching Exemplary, Commendable, Developing, and Comprehensive — based on what the state calls <a class="Link" href="https://www.isbe.net/summative" target="_blank" ><u>core and elevating indicators</u></a>.</p><p>“If you were a school district that had significant improvement from one year to the next, you could still be outperformed by another school and be kicked out of the Exemplary band, because only 10% of schools could be labeled as Exemplary under our old system,” Illinois State Superintendent of Education Tony Sanders said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe title="Search your Chicago school's summative designation" aria-label="Table" id="datawrapper-chart-uIcfZ" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/uIcfZ/5/" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="width: 0; min-width: 100% !important; border: none;" height="693" data-external="1"></iframe><script type="text/javascript">(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();</script> </div> </div></div><p>Although the categories aren’t exactly the same, the distribution of schools across the performance spectrum has shifted. Instead of labeling only the top 10% Exemplary, 27% of Illinois schools have earned the label. Last year, almost three-quarters of all Illinois public schools fell in the Commendable category, but with the introduction of a new second-highest ranking — Approaching Exemplary — Commendable schools make up a little more than a quarter of the total.</p><p>More Chicago schools are being considered Exemplary, with an increase from 2% of CPS schools in 2025 to 9% in 2026. The portion of schools in the bottom two rungs of the new ranking ladder also swelled compared to last year, when approximately 14% of CPS schools were in the two lowest categories. But CPS serves more students with higher needs, such as English learners and those from low income families.</p><p>The designations are helpful for assessing the state of student needs across the district, but they aren’t the end-all be-all, CPS deputy chief education officer Annise Lewis said. Internally, CPS <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2022/2/23/22948107/chicago-public-schools-school-ratings-sqrp-accountability/" target="_blank" ><u>no longer uses its old rating system</u></a> that assigned schools letter or number grades after the teachers union’s pushback that it disproportionately penalized schools that served more high-needs students. Under the district’s current strategic plan, academic outcomes share importance with other goals such as student growth and well-being, Lewis said.</p><h3>Proficiency trends up after Illinois cut score change </h3><p>All public school students <a class="Link" href="https://www.isbe.net/iar" target="_blank" ><u>in grades 3-8 take the Illinois Assessment of Readiness</u></a>. Students’ performance on the exam falls into one of four categories: above proficient, proficient, approaching proficient, and below proficient.</p><p>The state education board <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/08/13/illinois-approves-lower-cut-scores-on-state-exams/" target="_blank" ><u>voted unanimously to lower the cut scores</u></a> for the assessment in 2025, citing the need to match student abilities and reduce <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/08/12/illinois-proposes-new-cut-scores-for-state-standardized-tests/" target="_blank" ><u>one of the highest cut scores in the nation</u></a>. Several states had already lowered them after pandemic-related academic declines. The change means that state test scores diverge from a national test known as the Nation’s Report Card.</p><p>Nationally, 13-year-olds’ average scores in reading and math have <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/06/10/new-naep-scores-show-older-students-struggling-in-reading-and-math/" target="_blank" ><u>taken a nosedive since the pandemic</u></a>, whereas 9-year-olds are bouncing back with growth in both subjects. Between 2012 and 2025, the average score for 13-year-olds decreased by 7 points in reading and 15 in math.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe title="Public schools in Illinois and Chicago saw slight gains on some standardized tests" aria-label="Split Bars" id="datawrapper-chart-Td1cY" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Td1cY/7/" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="width: 0; min-width: 100% !important; border: none;" height="635" data-external="1"></iframe><script type="text/javascript">(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();</script> </div> </div></div><p>In Chicago, the percentage of students considered proficient in ELA increased by 3 percentage points to nearly 46% — a jump that paralleled the state’s gains. CPS Director of Literacy Jane Fleming attributes that performance to the district’s “standards aligned and culturally responsive” initiatives. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2024/10/17/cps-students-make-progress-on-standardized-exams-high-school-graduation-rates-are-flat/" target="_blank" ><u>increased proficiency</u></a> is especially impressive considering the district’s large English learner population, which also saw small gains, Fleming said.</p><p>IAR math proficiency is another story. The portion of students between third and eighth grade statewide who are considered proficient sits more than 15% lower than students who are proficient in ELA.</p><p>Illinois high schoolers did better in math than in ELA. All 11th grade students must take the college entrance exam, and this past spring, the cohort posted a higher composite math score at 19.2 than the 17.9 composite for ELA. The percentage of students considered proficient in ELA on the ACT dropped from 2025 to 2026.</p><h3><b>Students are missing less school, but still more than before pandemic</b> </h3><p>Chronic absenteeism dropped again, the fourth consecutive year of declines since it <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2025/chicago-public-schools-student-absenteeism-increases/" target="_blank" ><u>ballooned as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic</u></a>. However, the percentage of students experiencing chronic absenteeism — defined by the U.S. Department of Education as missing 10% of school days — is still higher than it was pre-2020. <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/01/13/chicago-public-schools-attedance-study-university-of-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>Numerous studies</u></a> outline how missing school can impact everything from test scores to a student’s sense of belonging.</p><p>This year, 23% of students outside Chicago were chronically absent, according to the new data. Since peaking at almost 45% in 2022, CPS’ chronic absenteeism rate has fallen about 6 percentage points. Vast racial disparities still persist — 44% of Black students were chronically absent this year compared to 23% of white students.</p><p>CPS chief of college and career success Megan Hougard said getting students to not miss school is the responsibility of everyone who works for the district, not just “one department in isolation.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe title="Chicago Public Schools sees dip in student absence rates, despite large rise since 2019" aria-label="Bar Chart" id="datawrapper-chart-bCrZK" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/bCrZK/10/" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="width: 0; min-width: 100% !important; border: none;" height="396" data-external="1"></iframe><script type="text/javascript">(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();</script> </div> </div></div><p><i>Makiya Seminera is a reporter covering how the state and federal government affect education in Chicago and across Illinois. Contact Makiya at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mseminera@chalkbeat.org" target="_blank" ><i>mseminera@chalkbeat.org</i></a><i>.</i></p><p><i>Kae Petrin is a data & graphics reporter who covers data related to K-12 education, voting rights, and public health for Civic News Company. Contact them at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:kpetrin@chalkbeat.org" target="_blank" ><i>kpetrin@chalkbeat.org</i></a><i>.</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Chalkbeat</i></a><i> is a nonprofit news organization covering public education.</i></p>

entries.title: Thief makes off with forklift from Daley Plaza in Loop, doesn't get far
entries.summary: <p>Someone jumped behind the wheel of a forklift in the Loop's Daley Plaza in the predawn hours but didn't get very far, Chicago police said. </p><p>The thief took the vehicle about 3:50 a.m. in the first block of West Washington Boulevard after entering a secure location and damaging a window, police said. </p><p>The forklift was found a short time later in the first block of West Madison Avenue, and no injuries were reported.</p><p>No one was arrested and Area 3 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: New Bears DT Jeffery Simmons: 2024 'Painted Nails' comment on QB Caleb Williams just 'smack talk'
entries.summary: <p>New <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons got his first taste of the fan base’s fervor leading up to the 2024 season when he took a shot at quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>. Simmons, then with the Titans, was asked by NFL Network’s Rich Eisen about facing Williams in his NFL debut and responded by jokingly calling him simply, “Painted Nails.”</p><p>The backlash from Bears fans was so strong that Simmons “thought they were going to crash my Instagram,” he said Friday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">“Painted nails.” - New Chicago Bear Jeff Simmons referring to Caleb Williams in 2024<a href="https://x.com/HGrahamNFL?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@HGrahamNFL</a> <a href="https://t.co/TxyaTpvMa3">pic.twitter.com/TxyaTpvMa3</a></p>— Chat Sports (@ChatSports) <a href="https://x.com/ChatSports/status/2115825800763314320?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Now they’re teammates, though, and Simmons said the jab at Williams two years ago was nothing more than trying to get under an opponent’s skin.</p><p>“I’ve been a fan of Caleb,” Simmons said after his first practice. “Of course, being on the other side and having to play against him, I’m not going to tell him that. I’m going to talk as much smack as I can.</p><p>“But now he’s on my team. Any teammate you ask about me, man, I have my teammate’s back, no matter if he’s on the other side of the ball or not. I’m going to talk the most smack to you when you’ve got a different color jersey on, but when we’re on the same team on Sundays, I go to war for any of my guys in the locker room. I hope Caleb would know that.”</p><p>Simmons said he had a nice exchange with Williams after the Bears and Titans held a joint practice in late August and again Friday morning before meetings.</p><p>“The comments a couple years ago about the nails is all part of my game, with the smack talk,” Simmons said. “I don’t know if you guys have heard, but I’m probably one of the best smack talkers. I talk a lot of smack when I’m on the field. I’m looking forward to being his teammate. We all know what type of player he is.”</p>

entries.title: Is expert criticism dead? Our new ‘Green Room’ video podcast weighs the question
entries.summary:
New from our Arts & Culture desk: the Green Room video podcast, which brings you closer to cultural conversations happening in Chicago and beyond. You can find it on YouTube, and we’ll keep our newsletter readers posted when there are new episodes.

Green Room Newsletter

You’re subscribed!

Please check your inbox for your confirmation.

Stay ahead of what’s hitting Chicago stages, galleries, museums and more with Green Room, WBEZ’s weekly arts & culture newsletter!

Sorry, there was an error registering your email.

By subscribing, you agree with WBEZ’s Terms of Use and Privacy Policy

Our first topic isn’t skimpy by any means: It’s about the withering state of expert criticism. Call it changes to technology, shorter attention spans or dwindling budgets at legacy media organizations: We're staring down the barrel of a long, intractable shift in the world of expert opinion.

In 2025 alone, the culture desk at the New York Times reassigned four of its critics to new roles, the Chicago Tribune eliminated its film critic position and, in our own newsroom, the Chicago Sun-Times offered acclaimed film critic Richard Roeper a buyout. But criticism has been deteriorating even before the TikTok age: A 2021 Pew Research study found that newsroom employment across the country has fallen by over a quarter since 2008, impacting the job prospects of columnists and critics.

Is all hope lost for expert opinions? We gathered WBEZ theater reporter and critic Mike Davis, food reporter and critic Maggie Hennessy and film critic Reggie Ponder to discuss the ever-changing media landscape, the role of critics and what the pros can learn from influencers.

Have any thoughts about the state of criticism? Or want to let us know what you would like to hear from us in our next episode? Send us a note at arts@wbez.org or leave a comment on YouTube.

entries.title: Bears practice report: Tight end Colston Loveland limited by neck injury
entries.summary: <p>What happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><p><b>Loveland concern</b></p><p>The newest issue for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>: tight end Colston Loveland was limited in practice Friday because of a neck injury. It’s his first time on an injury report in more than a year.</p><p>The injury comes just as Loveland was starting to heat up. After a slow start, he caught 13 passes for 134 yards and two touchdown catches.</p><p><b>Monangai still out</b></p><p>The Bears hoped the extended break between the Patriots and Seahawks games would give No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai a shot to get back on the field, but it looks like he’ll miss his fourth consecutive game with a toe injury. He missed practice again Friday.</p><p>Monangai had 324 yards and three touchdowns in the first four games as a complement to D’Andre Swift.</p><p><b>Corner office</b></p><p>The Bears might be OK at cornerback against the Seahawks on Monday as Tyrique Stevenson continued practicing through a hamstring injury and Malik Muhammad (toe) was limited.</p><p><b>Poles on Kmet</b></p><p>General manager Ryan Poles sounded hopeful to have tight end Cole Kmet back next season. Kmet is out the rest of this season with a knee injury and has a relatively affordable out in his contract for 2027, but Poles said the team is working to help him return to “original form” and “the best version of himself.”</p><p><b>Put it on his tab</b></p><p>The NFL fined Bears quarterback Caleb Williams $23,882 for wearing Caddix cleats against the Patriots last week. That’s double <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/25/bears-qb-caleb-williams-fined-11-941-for-wearing-tom-brady-backed-caddix-cleats-another-fine-likely-coming" >the fine he incurred for wearing them against the Falcons</a>.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: As Blackhawks search for solutions, Anton Frondell's usage could be one place to start
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' list of problems runs so long at the moment that it's clear no singular fix will turn things around. </p><p>Most of the problems are interconnected, too, making it impossible to isolate each one. The Hawks aren't scoring because they don't have the puck enough, which is because they don't defend well enough. But they can't overcome their flawed defense because they're not scoring.</p><p>General manager Kyle Davidson is likely wracking his brain for ideas after witnessing a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/29/blackhawks-red-wings-jeff-blashill-patrick-kane" >very discouraging loss</a> Thursday in Detroit. The Hawks canceled practice Friday, so their lineup Saturday against the Bruins won't be revealed until warmups.</p><p>Trade rumors are starting to trickle around, but the NHL market is far from robust this early in the season. Coach Jeff Blashill's job seems safe for the time being, despite fans' anger, but it's impossible to know for sure.</p><p>That leaves changes to the existing roster's composition or systems as the most viable short-term possibilities. </p><p>Blashill has already extensively experimented with line blending, discovering a few briefly promising combinations — like the Frank Nazar, Patrick Kane and Oliver Moore line — but nothing needle-moving yet. </p><p>The systems have remained the same since last season, so perhaps altering those could represent the next frontier. But that's difficult to do amid a stretch of nine games in 16 days. The next break in the schedule (Nov. 8-11) could be a critical juncture.</p><p>Strangely, one of the few Hawks who hasn't been involved whatsoever in Blashill's line blending is rookie Anton Frondell.</p><p>Frondell has been stapled to center — with veteran Tyler Bertuzzi stapled to his left wing — since training camp opened. That arrangement worked well early on, but its effectiveness has faded lately.</p><p>Blashill acknowledged Frondell was one of many Hawks who didn't skate or compete hard enough Thursday. That's now three games out of the last five in which Blashill has described Frondell's performance as subpar, and six straight games in which he hasn't recorded a point.</p><p>Blashill framed that as a "pretty good" 10:3 ratio of good vs. bad games for the 19-year-old Swede overall this season, but things are trending downward.</p><p>So is his ice time. He played less than 14:10 in each of those three bad games, including a career-low 11:44 on Thursday. Afterward, Blashill admitted he maybe "didn't give [him] enough of a chance to get out" of his funk.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">I liked this defensive shift from Anton Frondell in Detroit: <a href="https://t.co/Hfb7KzRMrm">pic.twitter.com/Hfb7KzRMrm</a></p>— Ben Pope’s Video Clips (@BenPopeCSTclips) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCSTclips/status/2116237886328602645?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 30, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>So why not try something different with Frondell? He's the type of big, talented forward who could potentially make a difference both offensively and defensively if reignited in the right situation. </p><p>Perhaps he's not ready to drive his own line for weeks upon weeks — particularly while handling <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/21/blackhawks-anton-frondell-ryan-greene-defensive-matchups" >tough matchups</a> against opposing stars every night — but is ready to dominate in a complementary role.</p><p>"He seems like he's been around a long time, but obviously he hasn't been," Ryan Donato said Thursday. "Lessons that you learn over time are really hard lessons, and it seems like he's already learned a lot of them. It's awesome to see."</p><p>Connor Bedard's wing opposite Roman Kantserov has been a carousel recently, with Kane, Ryan Greene and Teuvo Teravainen all getting looks there without success. That would be one obvious spot in which to slot Frondell if the Hawks are willing to simply try him on the wing. </p><p>Doing so wouldn't require abandoning their long-term vision of him potentially becoming a Jonathan Toews- or Aleksander Barkov-type center. It could be undone quickly if it doesn't work. In fact, they could even try Frondell at center and Bedard on the wing if so desired.</p><p>A different role could also possibly spark Bertuzzi, who's on pace for just 13 goals this season after burying 32 last season.</p><p>One way or another, the Hawks' strategy of spreading out their forward talent seems to be watering it down instead. It's time to try condensing it.</p>
entries.author: Ben Pope

entries.title: Kiss-cam controversy involving slew of suburban political figures draws lawsuit from conservative nonprofit
entries.summary: <p>The kiss-cam controversy in Lyons Township is heating up, with a lawsuit alleging that footage of the encounter and other relevant records were improperly withheld in violation of the state’s public records statute.</p><p>The elected clerk of Lyons Township government is Elyse Hoffenberg, who is responsible for handing requests to the agency for records under the Illinois Freedom of Information Act. That state law guarantees public access to public documents upon request, from paper and electronic records to videos.</p><p>Hoffenberg is also a Democratic candidate for Cook County Board, facing off against Republican Liz Gorman in Tuesday’s general election.</p><p>Hoffenberg, of La Grange, was captured on surveillance video inside the Lyons Township’s government offices in Countryside getting kissed after hours on July 13 by Bridgeview Mayor Steve Landek. He’s a former state senator, the Lyons Township’s Democratic committeeman and a longtime political ally of convicted ex-Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan (D-Chicago.)</p><p>Gorman and others got wind of the embrace, and under FOIA provisions requested a copy of related records including the video — something Hoffenberg initially wouldn’t release.</p><p>Later, she handed over a selected clip to news outlets, and has called the kiss inappropriate but also non-romantic.</p><p>Gorman, an Orland Park resident, has said whatever it was, it was inappropriate in a government building.</p><p>But Gorman said Lyons Township hadn't released all of what she requested, and a conservative nonprofit group based in Washington, D.C., Judicial Watch, followed up with a similar request on Aug. 31, but didn’t get a response.</p><p>Judicial Watch took the matter to court, filing a lawsuit in Cook County Sept. 28 against Lyons Township saying the state’s FOIA statute was violated. The law says requested records, in most cases, must be turned over within five business days.</p><p>“On information and belief, Defendant received Plaintiff’s emailed request the same day it was sent,” the lawsuit states. “To date, Defendant has failed to respond to Plaintiff’s request in any way or even acknowledge receipt of the request.”</p><p>In recent days, Hoffenberg turned over some information, while calling the earlier lack of a response "unintentional" and the result of "an administrative oversight," according to a letter from her township office to Judicial Watch's lawyer.</p><p>The letter also said: "I respectfully request that you confer with your client regarding voluntary dismissal of the claims for declaratory and injunctive relief insofar as they seek production of records that have been furnished. I further invite you to discuss an appropriate resolution of any remaining issues so that this matter may be concluded without unnecessary additional litigation or expense to either party."</p><p>But it's not yet clear whether the disclosed records represent all that Judicial Watch asked for. The group wouldn't comment.</p><p>Gorman suspects Hoffenberg tried delaying the release so it wouldn’t impact her election efforts.</p><p>“Now it’s going to be stuck to the taxpayers of Lyons Township,” Gorman said, referring to the legal fees needed to defend the case.</p><p>The law firm defending Lyons Township against the lawsuit includes attorney Burt Odelson, who has worked for Lyons Mayor Chris Getty on the governmental and political sides.</p><p>Getty, who’s also the Lyons Township supervisor and a candidate running in Tuesday’s election for Congress as an independent, is a political rival of Hoffenberg. She's accused him of leaking the initial footage to Gorman’s camp. Getty has denied that.</p><h3>Read the pending lawsuit below</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/5b/27/f55035bb462fb4c50f503eb77294/lyonslawsuit.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Read Lyons Township’s response</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b9/54/011d5d54417d90d594c21cc9d337/lyonsletter.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/09/kiss-cam-video-lyons-township-elyse-hoffenberg-steve-landek-chris-getty" target="_blank" >Kiss-cam video serves as backdrop to raucous public meeting in Lyons Township</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/28/lyons-township-elyse-hoffenberg-liz-gorman-cook-county-board-race-steve-landek-chris-getty" target="_blank" >Kiss-cam scandal brewing in Lyons Township between elected officials</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/31/lyons-mayor-chris-getty-campaign-loan-federal-tax-lien-state-elections-board" target="_blank" >In highly unusual move, Lyons mayor takes $245k loan from campaign committee to pay personal tax liability</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Sky did Angel Reese a favor by dealing her to Dream
entries.summary: <p>Things just ain’t the same. Since she left.</p><p>She just ain’t the same. Nothing is.</p><p>To see, watch, cheer for, hate, despise, accept Angel Reese playing in an unprecedented Game 7 for a WNBA championship is to have a hyperacute understanding of space and place.</p><p>How does Barbie have a Cinderella season? She leaves — or is traded, removed, exiled from, you choose — Chicago.</p><p>More societal than game-related. More community — as in area, location, population and populus, media, etc. — than basketball-related. Making her more aligned with ‘‘the dead internet theory’’ than probably any athlete alive. To act like all of the aforementioned hasn’t played a role in the chronicling of Angel Reese’s ascent would be inane.</p><p>But, then, why should anything less be expected of us when it comes to her?</p><p>Everything from her builds around the ‘‘UNAPOLOGETIC’’ tat that runs down the side of her left wrist. But now the mean mugs hit different, the ‘‘too smalls’’ hit different, the screams, yells, taunts heard differently, the beast-mode play, the F-bombs for further self-encouragement and esteem, the three-finger salutes when they drop, the ‘‘shots fired’’ gestures. All have led to a different type of acceptance by some for and still against Angel Reese, along with a different sense by which society has been forced to view, judge and assess her.</p><p>The Empress strikes back.</p><p>The major key: impacting winning. Which came with a perceived difference in acceptance by the Dream organization about who she is. By seeing passion in her actions instead of interpreting them as forms of petulance. There’s a silent and almost invisible self-efficacy within her that cannot be seen externally. Atlanta taught her how to hone and still own that in a way believed abandoned, if at all attempted, by the Sky.</p><p>The benefit of being around WNBA vets, a coaching staff and an organization that poured into her in a way that seems to have matured her five years over the course of a six-month season. As Angel likes to say: ‘‘This is what it looks like when purpose meets the moment.’’ She literally used the word ‘‘joy’’ to describe what she and her squad needed to play with to win the final game of the Finals.</p><p>A word that has not been heard or associated with the Sky since James Wade foretold the organization’s future and nascenced the free fall.</p><p>NBC’s Zora Stevenson leaned in on the fact that it seems Reese ‘‘fits with this team.’’ It’s so much more. Reese fits with Atlanta’s culture. She fits with their people, their life mattering in what they both historically and currently represent and their comfort in the skin they’re in. She fits with everything she has grown to believe and mean when it comes to Black success and the strive to find it in America.</p><p>Chicago, in many parts and areas, wasn’t (and oftentimes isn’t when it comes to accepting sports leaders) the place for that. The Sky, as they currently stand as a franchise in the WNBA, weren’t the organization capable of cultivating that. The media, unused to seeing an overt-spoken leader of one of our professional teams, wasn’t prepared for a young, cultural, superstar athlete to not conform to or not cower under the demands publicly put upon them to be something and someone different.</p><p>Briefly noted, the physicality of the Finals perfectly suited Angel. It showed in the first three games, where ‘‘Finals MVP’’ began to orbit around her name. It showed in Games 4<br>and 5, where she showcased how much of a not-finished product she still is. The essence of her being the face of a team playing for the championship revealed itself in Games 6 and 7. All that she is, for the world to see, on display on the highest, most coveted stage in the game.</p><p>A stage we all must openly admit she may have never seen had she remained here, in this city, unable to shake the proximity of the shadow of Caitlin Clark, had they — the Sky — not gifted her by no longer believing in her.</p><p>The basketball part changed. The expectations changed. A different commitment to the game born. The results were a result of those. And anyone believing that she (or Gabby Williams, who was drafted by the Sky in 2018 and has, since being traded in 2021, won silver medals in the Olympics and the FIBA World Cup, become a two-time WNBA All-Star, made three WNBA All-Defensive teams and become the face of a two-year old franchise in the WNBA Finals) would have turned into the player she has become had she remained here needs to be given a Ph.D. in mythomania.</p><p>Her aura awareness risen. Defiance, more accepted or less misunderstood? She called this ‘‘the year of simplicity. Less is more.’’ This year of her 24. She’s where she belongs.</p><p>She made the world smell her perfume. The deep divide that existed between she and we? She no longer has to battle. The benefit of the doubt that didn’t exist from before she got to the ‘‘W’’ that seemed to carry over to her entire time here in Chicago? Finally decided to bless her with the space and place she craved once she got to the ATL.</p><p>Home.</p><p>It allowed Angel Reese to finally dream.</p>

entries.title: White Sox face a new challenge this winter — improving a contender
entries.summary: <p>In the first three offseasons of Chris Getz’s tenure as White Sox general manager, a move bolstering the <i>organizational infrastructure</i> like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/29/white-sox-hiring-matt-roffe-away-from-brewers-to-fill-open-amateur-scouting-director-role" target="_blank" ><u>hiring Matt Roffe from the Brewers to run their drafts</u></a> might have been a signature moment.</p><p>The Sox amateur scouting department grew increasingly aggressive and successful in pursuing prep talent in recent years. But until they’re turning late-round dice rolls into valuable prospects at the rate the Brewers have–and until they’re reaping the returns of an overhauled international amateur operation under David Keller, whose best work won’t join the organization until the 2028 and 2029 IFA classes–the endless depth enjoyed in Milwaukee even as star players walk out the door in free agency will remain hard to replicate.</p><p>That will just make this coming offseason more vital.</p><p>The reward for one of the most satisfying seasons in franchise history is everyone takes the White Sox seriously now, and the expectations are for impact player acquisitions alongside the structural improvements. The Sox feel good about their seven-figure investments in high school shortstops like Caleb Bonemer and Billy Carlson helping down the road–<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/22/the-white-sox-have-openings-in-the-outfield-and-slugging-prospect-caleb-bonemer-is-preparing-to-fill-one" target="_blank" ><u>or sooner</u></a>–but Getz noted at last August’s trade deadline that his farm system lacked the “<i>middle class</i>” prospects behind them that get deals done.</p><p>“I didn't want to give up our top-end talent for rentals, I didn't want to do that this particular trade deadline,” Getz said, after just one of the four players he acquired made the ALDS roster. “Did I want to do more? I did, and that's where I find comfort in it. Because I was willing to do more. It just wasn't there.”</p><p>That’s less of an impediment to the club’s necessary starting pitching pursuits this winter, as free agency is an option.</p><p>After traveling to Houston to celebrate his team’s series victory, Sox chairman Jerry Reinsdorf was also in Cleveland for their Game 5 defeat, thanking his dejected players as they walked off the field for a season that revitalized the fan base. That sentiment, and the improved television ratings and a half-million jump in attendance, should carry over some to Reinsdorf’s discussions of next season’s budget with Getz, with many in the industry expecting an active market ahead of an anticipated lockout when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.</p><p>“There's talent in the free-agent group, there is,” Getz said of the starting pitching market. “We've got payroll flexibility, it's a young growing team. There's going to be opportunities to add, the timing of that, who knows. We're at the mercy of a lot of different things.”</p><p>Things like the specter of a shortened season hanging around to discourage pushing forward at full force for 2027. Chasing Tarik Skubal to potentially record-setting prices for starting pitching hasn’t been the Sox MO under Reinsdorf, nor a front office that regularly discusses the realities of scouring for undervalued commodities with a below-average payroll. There are some potential mid-rotation fits in free agency, but the overall class is shallow, and the market of pitchers coming stateside from East Asian leagues that has brought Erick Fedde and Anthony Kay to the South Side in previous years is viewed by the Sox as being less robust this winter.</p><p>If history is any indication, some activity is simply coming due to the calendar.</p><p>There are other candidates, but infielder William Bergolla Jr. is probably the only must-add player for a full White Sox 40-man roster by the Nov. 17 deadline for protecting players for the Rule 5 draft. And five years ago, the previous lockout canceled the Rule 5 draft when it stretched into spring.</p><p>But unless teams are informed otherwise at the General Managers’ meetings the week before, it’s expected to be business as usual, which will mean a wealth of player movement as teams clear out space on the 40-man roster. At the same deadline last year, the Sox swung two trades to add three players. Two years prior, it precipitated a five-for-one trade sending Aaron Bummer to Atlanta. The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players comes three days later on Nov. 20, deepening the free-agency pool as teams shed costly commitments.</p><p>Sifting through spare parts from other teams’ 40-man rosters can sound like small potatoes, but it’s a substantial part of how the 2026 team was built, and they’ll need to resourcefully replenish depth similar to how organizations they admire in Milwaukee and Tampa regularly do.</p><p>For the first time in a while, the White Sox cohere as a unit more than they impress on paper.</p><p>That’s a compliment to all involved, but also lends itself to a winter where there’s plenty of room for improvement. There’s a promising young core, but relatively few immovable mainstays. How and when to add to a team seemingly on the rise is a question other up-and-comers have struggled with in this spot.</p><p>But again, this is the reward for winning.</p><p>“It's definitely something you need to be mindful of, [and] as we've continued to develop our research and development group and understand our projections and the future production of our players, that objective information is vital in making those decisions,” Getz said. “I've talked about maintaining this identity of the clubhouse and what has made this group special. Players evolve, things evolve, incentives evolve. I feel like we've got a really strong group to be able to recognize when change needs to happen.”</p>

entries.title: Controversial DOJ boss takes reins in tainted ‘Broadview 6’ case, stymies judge’s inquiry
entries.summary: <p>A controversial top Justice Department official inserted himself into Chicago's "Broadview Six" case Friday, insisting "the United States has not agreed to provide any information"<b> </b>sought by a judge who might name a special prosecutor<b> </b>to look into wrongdoing by the feds.</p><p>Associate Attorney General Stanley<b> </b>Woodward<b> </b>asked U.S. District Judge April Perry to clarify if she meant for her recent records "request" to be a "directive." However, he added, "the United States believes further proceedings would not be appropriate."</p><p>Woodward's entry into the case followed the withdrawal Friday of two local federal prosecutors on the case, Assistant U.S. Attorneys Diane MacArthur and Nathaniel Whalen.</p><p>Woodward, the Justice Department’s third<b> </b>highest-ranking official, previously served as senior counselor to President Donald Trump. </p><p>But he’s increasingly finding himself at the center of the agency’s national controversies. He faced off earlier Friday with a federal judge<b> </b>in Washington who pressed him on whether the Trump administration had been trying to evade her review, according to news reports.</p><p>His name appears at the top of the Justice Department’s recent<b> </b>lawsuit over possible results<b> </b>in the Alaska Senate<b> </b>race. And back in May, he<b> </b>signed<b> </b>the settlement agreement between<b> </b>the<b> </b>president<b> </b>and the IRS that established the controversial “anti-weaponization fund”<b> </b>for people who claimed to be harmed by “lawfare” and the weaponization of the justice system.</p><p>Woodward's entry into Chicago's "Broadview Six" case came with a Friday<b> </b>deadline<b> </b>looming<b> </b>for the feds<b> </b>to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/01/broadview-six-perry-boutros-mecklenburg" >turn over records</a><b> </b>sought by<b> </b>Perry. She is still considering whether to name a special prosecutor<b> </b>to investigate Boutros and other Justice Department officials<b> </b>for criminal contempt. </p><p>“My sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me," Perry said during an Oct. 1 hearing.</p><p>Perry<b> </b>later<b> </b>asked the feds<b> </b>to turn over<b> </b>records<b> </b>by Friday<b> </b>that could shed light on whether<b> </b>Boutros' team<b> </b>communicated<b> </b>with anyone outside his office about the case, and whether Boutros knew<b> </b>last fall about<b> </b>apparent misconduct<b> </b>by his staff before a grand jury.</p><p>The judge characterized her inquiry as a "request," though. That raised questions about whether it counts as a formal order.</p><p>The “Broadview Six” case <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" >revolved around a protest</a> outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" name="image-800000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/899076a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/359e441/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The so-called "Broadview Six." Clockwise from top left: Michael Rabbitt, Brian Straw, Kat Abughazaleh, Andre Martin, Joselyn Walsh and Catherine “Cat” Sharp." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/98b90b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3051x1712+0+161/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F39%2Fa6%2F95a93ed84dbeac8e1812670fb181%2Fbroadview6-comp.jpg"
